PHSCS 587

Bands, states and holes

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how promoting a valence electron creates two mobile excitations

A device needs mobile charge, and its band structure determines which electronic states can carry it. The figure separates the conduction-band edge EC from the valence-band edge EV by the bandgap Eg = EC − EV. These are electron energies, commonly measured in electronvolts (eV). An ideal bulk bandgap contains no allowed extended band states; defects can introduce additional states that need a separate model.

Each individual quantum state, including its spin label, can hold at most one electron. A spatial orbital can often accommodate two opposite-spin states. Filling an entire valence band produces no net transport current in equilibrium because the occupied states have balancing velocities. Exciting an electron into the conduction band leaves an unoccupied valence state that can move through successive electron rearrangements.

That missing valence electron is described as a hole with positive charge +q, where q = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A conduction electron carries −q. Hole concentration p counts missing valence electrons per volume; conduction-electron concentration n counts electrons in conduction-band states. A hole is a band-dependent excitation, rather than a second positively charged fundamental particle.

Example

An above-gap optical excitation can create one conduction electron and one valence hole. Initially Δn = Δp, although contacts, trapping and recombination can subsequently change their spatial distributions.

Practice

1. Why does the two-electron capacity of a spatial orbital agree with the exclusion principle?

Include spin in the state label.

Opposite spins label two distinct single-electron states. Each complete state still has occupancy zero or one.

2. What remains after a conduction electron recombines with a valence hole?

Track both excitations.

The valence vacancy is filled and the conduction excitation disappears. Energy is transferred to light, lattice vibrations or another carrier, depending on the mechanism.
